newsitem.title: USA: 'Marathon man' Dole campaigns deep into night.
newsitem.headline: 'Marathon man' Dole campaigns deep into night.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole -- a self-described "marathon man" -- campaigned through the night and into early Saturday morning, traveling around Michigan by plane, bus and truck on his non-stop push to Election Day.
Dole traveled from Grand Rapids to Detroit along highway I-96 -- symbolic of his 96-hour final push to the election on Tuesday in which he hopes to unseat President Bill Clinton.
"Keep on truckin'," a chipper Dole yelled out to reporters as he stepped out of his bus, "Asphalt 1, the American Dream," and into the cab of an 18-wheeled tractor-trailer outside of Grand Rapids.

Once in Detroit, Dole will travel in the pre-dawn hours on Saturday to Newark, New Jersey, and then on to Philadelphia. Dole plans to hit at least 14 states by Election Day when he ends campaigning in his hometown of Russell, Kansas, where he and his wife Elizabeth Dole plan to vote.

Riding shotgun in the truck rig with driver Skip Reiffer, Dole wore a white leather jacket that said "Republican leader" and called himself "marathon man" as he tried to communicate with other truckers over a CB, or shortwave, radio.
"Hey fellas, this is marathon man, marathon man," Dole said over the radio. No one responded immediately.
Reiffer, whose truck was emblazoned "Industrial Building Supply," was asked what he was hauling and Dole shot out a quick reply, "absentee ballots." The cargo was actually conveyor belts.
The truck was led by a state police convoy and followed by a caravan of at least 12 vans and buses carrying staff, photographers and Secret Service agents.
After about 20 minutes in the truck, Dole climbed back onto his bus for the ride to a truck stop restaurant, bowling alley and a rally before hundreds of cheering well-wishers.
At the pre-midnight rally in Brighton, Michigan, Dole continued his barrage against Clinton's ethics. "I have never seen such arrogance," Dole said of the Clinton White House.
The 73-year-old candidate hopes the exhausting schedule will generate enough enthusiasm to overcome polls showing him behind President Bill Clinton.
The around-the-clock campaigning, which Dole calls his "non stop victory tour," began early Friday in Columbus and Ashland, Ohio.

From Ohio, Dole flew to Grand Rapids for a rally with former Presidents George Bush and Gerald Ford and Michigan Republican Gov. John Engler, who said he saw "the enthusiasm levels climbing higher" for the Republican candidate.
"You start to get a sense that something is going on -- you get a sense of a shift," said Engler.
Dole seemed fired up at the rally with Bush and Engler and told a boisterous crowd of several thousand, "I think I smell victory in the air."
